Bill (No. 135) to amend the Immigration Act-Mr. Oliver-read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
We have not had much explanation with regard to the object of this proposed legislation. Perhaps the minister will take this opportunity of giving it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The purpose of this amendment is to make further provision in regard to the exclusion of immigrants. The Act as it stands contains provisions for the protection of immigrants and also for the exclusion and deportation of immigrants. An immigrant arriving at a Canadian port, if considered to be undesirable according to the terms of our immigration law, may be excluded at that port, and if excluded under the terms of the law the transportation company which brought him to the Canadian port must take him back to the port from which he sailed, and the country in which that port is situated must receive him back, because until he has officially landed in Canada he is still to all intents and purposes a resident of the country from which he sails. If an undesirable comes into Canada and it becomes necessary or desirable to deport him, we call upon the steamship company which brought him to Canada to take him back to the port from which he sailed. But if he is not a citizen of the country in which that port is situated, that country does not need to receive him back, and it is not possible for the steamship company to carry out our order of deportation. We were, therefore, in the position of having possibly to deal with numbers of people whom it might be desirable to deport, and yet because of their not having sailed from the country of their citizenship, or not having come from that country by a ticket upon which we could hold the transportation company responsible to take them back to the country of their citizenship, we were not in a position to deport them. In order then that the intent of the immigration law might be carried out and made effective in regard to the exclusion of undesirables, it was provided by a regulation passed on the 8th of January last that immigrants arriving from a country other than that of their citizenship might under certain circumstances be excluded. This regulation was put in force and was applied to the
arrivals of Asiatics on the Pacific coast, in one instance, to Japanese coming from the Sandwich islands, and in another case to Hindus coming from Hong Kong. There is a large Japanese population in the Sandwich islands who, for industrial or commercial reasons, are looking for another field of settlement. These people, having left the country of their citizenship, having become residents of the Sandwich islands, which are dependencies of the United States, and then having decided to come to Canada, were not under the jurisdiction of the country of their citizenship. If we had reason to order their deportation and to order the steamship company to take them back into the Sandwich islands, the United States government could refuse to receive them. They were then in the position in which they were when they came from the Sandwich islands and we practically hand to let them land. The same condition prevailed in regard to the movement from Hong Kong. Large numbers of Hindus who have left India and settled in Hong ICong, for one reason or another desired to settle in Canada. The question, in fact, came up in the first place, because of our finding it desirable to deport a number of these Hindus who had landed in Vancouver. They were subject to the deportation clauses of the Immigration Act, but when we undertook to deport them the government of Hong Kong refused to receive them because they were not citizens of that dependency and they were simply left on our hands. The regulation of the 8th of January, passed to meet that case, was put in force and was applied to the arrivals from the Sandwich islands and from other regions in the Pacific. It was in March that the large arrivals of Hindus from Hong Kong took place. The regulation was applied to these people, legal proceedings were taken by the transportation company to set aside the regulation, and it was set aside by the courts of British Columbia as not having been in proper form. The point taken was that while the Governor in Council had the right to exclude, he had not the right to delegate that power of exclusion to the Minister of the Interior as had been done by the terms of the regulation ; therefore, the regulation was declared to be of non-effect and these people had to be permitted to land. We passed the regulation again so as to conform with the decision of the court and it is now in force, but we believe that this question is of such importance in the administration of our immigration law that it should be embodied in the law itself, and should not be dependent upon a regulation. Therefore the section which is contained in the Bill was drafted and is brought before the House for its approval. I might say that since the Bill was drafted some exception has been taken to the use of a certain word

in the latter part of the clause and it has been thought advisable to redraft the latter part of the section. I have an amendment here which I desire to propose and which has been approved by the Department of Justice. I would move :
That all the words after the word ' who ' in the fourth line be struck out and that the following be inserted in lieu thereof: 'have come to Canada otherwise than by continuous journey from the country of which they are natives or citizens and upon through tickets purchased in such country.'

The object of the Bill is to extradite Hindus whose case is not otherwise covered by the regulations from British Columbia to the place of their origin. These Hindus, as the hon. gentleman has mentioned, are British subjects coming from either- India or Hong Kong. Have we the power to extradite them for any other reason than for quarantine purposes ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This provision is for the purpose of saving us the trouble of extraditing them. It is to enable us to exclude them under certain conditions.
Can you for any other-purpose than that of quarantine exclude a British subject from coming into the country ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is a matter that I am hardly in a position to answer, but inasmuch as the immigration law has been on the statute-book since- the session of 1906 and has been applied to a very large number of cases not only in excluding, or deporting, or extraditing, which is the word that my hon. friend uses, and has never been called in question, I presume that we have the necessary authority.
I doubt it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend suggested that this provision was made especially to apply to Hindus. That is incorrect. It applies to all people. I instanced the case of the Hindus as being one in which it was necessary and desirable to apply the provision.

I do not quite understand the necessity of the legislation. The law as it stands at present is as follows :
The Governor in Council may, by proclamation or order, whenever he considers it necessary or expedient, prohibit the landing in Canada of any specified class of immigrants of which due notice shall be given to the transportation company.
The Governor in council, by order made on the 8th of January, 1908, undertook to delegate to the Minister of the Interior the power which was conferred on the Governor in Council by the statute which I have Mr. OLIVER.
just read. The operative words of the order in council are as follows :
The Governor in Council is pleased to order, and it is hereby ordered, that whenever, in the opinion of the Minister of the Interior, the condition of the labour market in Canada is such as to make the application of section 20 of the Immigration Act desirable, or, whenever, in the opinion of the Minister of the Interior, other conditions exist which, in a special degree render necessary the application of sections 26 to 30 inclusive of the said Act, immigrants may be prohibited from landing or coming into Canada unless they come from the country of their birth or citizenship by a continuous journey and on through tickets purchased before leaving the country of their birth or citizenship.
Then the matter came before Mr. Justice Clements, of British Columbia, upon proceedings in habeas corpus, and Mr. Justice Clements did not set aside the order in council -of course he could not do that-but he declared that the order iu council was not valid inasmuch as the Privy Council had seen fit to delegate to the Minister of the Interior a power which could only be exercised by the Governor in Council himself. And so the men, as I understand, were released on habeas corpus. I do not observe, nor have I heard from the Minister of the Interior that there has been any difficulty of such a character as would render this legislation necessary. If it is necessary well and good, but I have not so far been able to ascertain what the necessity is. The necessity could only arise if the words, ' any specified class of immigrants,' do not include the conditions which are provided for in this Bill. No such argument has been made so far as I am aware, and no such decision has been given, and therefore I am not yet able to understand the necessity for the legislation. In other words there would have been no difficulty at air in the court, so far as we know, if the Governor in Council had made the order in the proper way instead of delegating the subject to the Minister of the Interior. At the present time the Governor in Council has passed the necessary order and the matter seems to be provided for in that way. Why is it then that we are asked to pass this legislation ? I am not speaking by way of criticism, but entirely for the purpose of information.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The reason for the legislation as I understand it is this : under the Immigration Act we have power to exclude and to deport certain immigrants who do not come up to a certain standard either physically, intellectually or morally, and whom we deem to be unworthy of Canadian citizenship. We have power to deport Hindus or any one else if we are of opinion that they come within any of the classes I have referred to. But suppose a Hindu who was physically or morally unfit came from Hong Kong but not from India, we

could exclude him or deport him. We can send him back on the steamship which has brought him and the steamer would take him to Hong Kong but the Hong Kong authorities would say: That man does not belong to us and we will not receive him. It is to obviate this that the law makes it another cause of exclusion if the man does not come direct from the land of his origin on a through ticket. We are creating another cause of exclusion in addition to the causes I have just mentioned, and this being made a cause of exclusion the transportation company understands it and they bring such a man here at their own risk and we will have the power to compel the company to take that man back.
I do not see how it will assist the situation if that is the real object of the statute.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is the object as I understand it.

Suppose an idiot or a person afflicted with a loathsome disease is taken on board at Hong Kong, you can now refuse him permission to land without this proposed statute. This Bill merely provides another reason on account of which he cannot land and you send him back in this case just as you did before. What is the advantage of it ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As long as we are aware that he is subject to the exclusion conditions of the Act at the port of landing we can exclude him as matters stand at present and there is no difficulty. But suppose we are not aware of this and we allow him to actually land and afterwards we find he is physically or mentally tainted, or financially unable to provide for his own support, any of these are causes for exclusion or deportation. For instance, a perfectly healthy Hindu leaves India, he comes to Hong Kong, finds matters do not suit him there, and he decides to come to British Columbia. He lands in British Columbia a perfectly healthy man mentally and physically, and we permit him to land but conditions are such that he lias no money, that he cannot get any work, and he becomes a public charge; he is subject to deportation under the terms of our immigration law, but if we undertake to deport him, under the terms of the law we arrest him, we compel the steamship company to take him on board, the steamship company takes him to Hong Kong and the Hong Kong government says: He does not belong to us, we will not admit him to our country and we will not allow him to land in Hong Kong. The only recourse in that case is that he. must be brought back to Canada and allowed to remain in Canada. Under such circumstances we cannot enforce our own law in regard to our own country.
Does the minister mean that this statute is intended to apply to persons who have landed in Canada ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: People who will land in Canada after the statute is passed.

That is not the reading of the statute at all. The reading of the statute is this: The Governor in Council may prohibit the landing in Canada. It does not deal with persons who having landed in Canada are found to be subject to such disabilities as would make it advisable to deport him. This statute is intended to prohibit certain persons from landing in Canada. I am sincerely trying to find out what good purpose the statute is intended to serve.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am trying to explain it. I try to tell my hon. friend how the case arises which makes it necessary for us to adopt the principle contained in the Bill. I have shown that under the terms of our Act as it stands to-day we are not able to protect ourselves as it was intended that we should protect ourselves. If this Act is passed, the man who goes on board a ship at Hong Kong, with a ticket bought at Hong Kong, if he is not a citizen of Hong Kong, can be prevented from landing in Canada.

The man who goes on board the steamer at Hong Kong may belong to one of two classes-he may be a perfectly good citizen, unexceptionable in every way, or he may be a person who is impecunious or idiotic or suffering from some disease on account of which we should exclude him. Is this intended to apply to one or to both of these classes. If only to one, to which one?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is intended to apply to all classes.
Why is it intended to apply to a man who would be a perfectly good citizen of this country?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Because we want to be in a position to protect ourselves against the man who will not be a good citizen of the country-not necessarily because of any inherent defect in himself, but because of conditions which may exist, and which do not admit of his being able to make a living in Canada.

Within the last couple of weeks a German went on board a vessel at New Zealand and went to Vancouver; but he was not allowed to land because he did not come from the country of his origin. There was no contention that he was not a good citizen; but he was excluded, and was forced to go to the United States.

Is it the intention by this Bill to exclude from this coun-

try every person who does not come from the country of his origin? If so, it seems to me that you will get into a lot of trouble. Another thing: I notice that by the regulation people coming from Europe must come by way of Portland or direct to a Canadian port.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, they may come through any port. Cases of hardship have arisen under the application of the regulation, because our officers have not thoroughly understood how we desired to apply it. But there is no difficulty whatever in regard to people who are coming to Canada through another country or by various lines of conveyance. It is quite customary for a man, say at a point in Central Europe, to buy a through ticket from that point to Canada. It matters not through how many countries he passes, we receive him. As he has a ticket from the country of his citizenship, we can compel the transportation company to take him back there, which we could not do if he had not that ticket.
The man I refer to was not a naturalized citizen of New Zealand, but he was a German who had lived there for several years. He was excluded because he did not come direct from Germany.
I think the object of the amendment brought in by the minister is quite plain.
To exclude Hindus, that is all.
Yes, to exclude Hindus and ail kinds of Asiatics, and all kinds of undesirable people.
Will it not exclude desirable classes as well?
Possibly if we gain in one respect we may suffer in another. In the case the hon. gentleman speaks of, I fancy the good sense of the immigration officer would allow the German to come in.
That is giving a good deal of latitude to the immigration officer.
If I or my hon. friend were an immigration officer, we would use the good sense the Lord has given us. We thought we had the positive power to exclude Orientals coming from India via Hong Kong.
What about the Japanese?

The arrangement entered into between Japan and Canada is working very well; we have no more Japanese coming into the country. That matter has been satisfactorily arranged-perhaps not as radically as some of ns would have Mr. U. WILSON.
liked to have had it arranged, but it is working well. Just as the Japanese were making Hawaii a bridge, so the Hindus have been making Hong Kong a bridge. There are a considerable number of Hindu policemen in Hong Kong; and these men, while a good looking Jot, are the most objectionable class of people we can get into our country. A good many of them while in Hong Kong lived on prostitution. The prostitutes of Hong Kong, the greatest shipping port in the world, stood in with them, and divided up their profits with them.
There must have been a large body of police.

Yes.
Mr. SAJI, HUGHES. How many thousands?

I speak of the first people who came. They are a most objectionable and undesirable class. The Hindus themselves do not want them. This clause will absolutely prohibit this class of people coming to our shores. It is purely and simply a restriction on Asiatics. The Japanese cannot come in by the Sandwich Islands or by Mexico. There has been a good deal of talk about these men having been British soldiers and wearing medals on their breasts. The men who managed to get over the order in council and furnish them with tickets purporting that they came from Calcutta, would be able to get silver medals for them without any trouble. I know very well that nine-tenths of them never saw any active service in India for the British empire. I think this clause is absolutely necessary if we are going to succeed in keeping these very undesirable people out of the country.

I would like to ask the minister if it is not a fact that a great deal of so-called American immigration consists of men from Scandinavia who remain a few years in the United States and then cross over to Canada?
They became citizens.
Not necessarily, unless they took the oath of allegiance.
They generally do.
I venture to say that a good many do not.

To return to the point raised a few moments ago by the leader of the opposition, what is the object of this legislation? Is it to add to the cases of exclusion those who come from somewhere else than their native country? At present we have a certain list of cases of exclusion and probably this Bill is intended to add to them. The Bill provides that:

30. The Governor in Council may, by proclamation or order, whenever he considers it necessary or expedient, prohibit the landing in Canada of any specified class of immigrants any immigrants who being natives or citizens of any specified country have come to Canada otherwise than by a continuous journey from that country on through tickets purchased there.
As I understand the present law, the fact that an English immigrant comes here from France is not a cause of exclusion, but it may be a cause for exclusion under this Bill. All that is required is a proclamation of the Governor in Council.
.Mr- GALLIHER. As I understand it the difference is this : Take a Hindu coming from Hong Kong to Vancouver, he may be Vancouver he will be allowed to land at all. The steamship company will have to take him back. But if he is a desirable immigrant and comes direct from India to \ ancouver be will be allowed to land though he may be deported later should he become one of the class subject to deportation. Then you can compel the steamship company to take him back to his own country and his own country is bound to receive him. You are consequently not in the position you would be in when deporting the same man who came from Hong Kong to Vancouver, because Hong Ivong not being his native country, it would not be bound to take him back.

We may be going much further than the government intend. I am not going to discuss the question of Hindus or Japanese for the moment. It will be possible under this to have Hindus, British subjects from Hong Kong, deported or not permitted to land, and Japanese direct from Japan permitted to land. That is what it means if it means anything. It may be most desirable, and no doubt it is, to limit the immigration of certain classes, but it is necessary to see that we are not going too far. One hon. gentleman suggests that the enforcement or non-enforcement shall be left to the discretion of the immigration officers. I do not think that is very desirable.
I do not think I suggested that.

I accept my hon. friend's assurance in that regard. But if such a suggestion has been made, I would be prepared to repudiate it. You cannot make laws and then invite your own officers to wilfully and knowingly break them. If this law is to be enacted, we must see that it is enforced in every part of Canada. What then will be the result? I agree with my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) that it distinctly proposes to add an additional cause of exclusion at the discretion of the Governor in Council. That is to say. any citizen coming from any country other than that of his birth or citizenship shall not
be allowed to land, although he may be in every other possible respect a most desirable citizen. You are aiming at a certain object, but you are accomplishing a good deal more than you aim at. Suppose Scandinavians go into the United States and do not become American citizens, and then propose to come and settle in this country, they are excluded by this order in council apparently because they do not come direct from the land of their birth or citizenship. Suppose these men have lived in the British isles a number of years and then come to Canada, they cannot be permitted to land under this order in council for the same reason. Germans coming here from the British islands or the United States would be exactly in the same category. Therefore, you are proposing a very drastic, comprehensive and far reaching amendment to our immigration laws. Your amendment may accomplish a certain purpose which you have in mind, but It may also accomplish some others you have not in mind.
This is evidently intended to get at the transportation companies.
No.

Take the case of a Hindu who comes here from Hong Kong, you may send him back on the steamer and he will not be allowed to land at Hong Kong. I do not think this will help the matter. Why does the hon. minister not bring in a law covering that aspect of the case? This will exclude any man coming from any country other than that of his birth or adoption. Personally I would much prefer a Hindu who has served the empire in the armies of Great Britain to a galvanized Yankee who has been an anarchist in his own land and has come to the United States where he has done his best to disrupt that republic, and who, if he crosses over to Canada. seeks in many instances to disrupt the established laws of the Dominion. I must say that a Hindu who has served in the British army and has had the discipline of a soldier is much more likely to make a good citizen of Canada, much more likely to upbuild the welfare, morality and dignity of this country than many of the class of animals who are imported
Order.

No 'order' about it. Many of these are not worthy the name of human beings. But these people are admitted, while soldiers who have served in the British army are excluded, not allowed to land and turned adrift. I move in amendment the following :-
Always excepting such immigrants as have served in the regular or auxiliary forces of the empire under the British flag.

I have not yet had a clear explanation from the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) or the Minister of the

Interior (Mr. Oliver) as to the effect of this proposed law. I may be wrong in my law, but I stated-and I have seen no reason yet to change my opinion-that this parliament cannot deprive a British subject of his allegiance or of his right to land in this country except for certain causes. He must not be excluded under the quarantine laws-that is he must not be diseased, idiotic or subject to lunacy:	Nor must he be
a criminal. Nor must he be an indigent person-our right in this case is similar to that exercised under the poor law of Great Britain of removing people from one parish to another. As I understand the Prime Minister, the law applies only to these classes, but, according to the Minister of the Interior, it goes further. Under the principle stated by the Minister of the Interior, this parliament could exclude any one. It is proposed that the Hindus shall be excluded, not because they are Hindus ; their crime consists in not coming direct from Hindustan, but in landing in a British colony on the way. I may have old-fashioned ideas as to the power of this country to deprive a British subject of his allegiance or of his rights as a British subject. I do not think that this parliament can do either.
How about Australia ?

I do not care about Australia. I do not know about the Australian law, though it may be such as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Macpberson) says. But my ground is that we cannot deprive a British subject of his allegiance or of his right as a British subject, provided lie is not a criminal, is not physically or mentally diseased and has money to pay his way.
Does not the hon. gentleman (Mr. Haggart) think that the Canadian parliament is paramount in tliese matters ? Has it not the highest possible powers within its jurisdiction ?

That is the very ground I take-that the power is not vested in this parliament, but that this is one of the reserve powers under the British North America Act. I may be wrong in my law. But, suppose we had the power that is claimed, is it judicious or right for us to legislate against British subjects in any other part of the empire ? Is it in the interest of this country or of the empire as a whole ? While it is right that we should protect ourselves against immigration tnat Is detrimental to the interests of the country, when a man is a good subject of the empire in one part of it, he has the right to all the privileges as a subject of the empire on landing in this country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think on reflection, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Haggart)) will agree with me that he has car-Mr. HAGGART.	;
ried a principle which is very good in itself a little too far. He says that we have not the power to close the door of this country against a British subject except for purposes of quarantine. Now we have as much power over British subjects coming from across the sea as we have over those in this country. At the present time, if a man is insane, even though a British subject, we have the right to put him in con-iinemeflt.
I admitted that principle-that idiots, lunatics, criminals and paupers might be excluded. I said that the common law of England provided for that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend stated that we had no power to exclude men except for purpose of quarantine.
I went further.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman will see that we have the power to exclude those who are physically tainted, section 28 of the Immigration Act provides :
Nq person shall be permitted to land in Canada who is a pauper, or destitute, a professional beggar, or vagrant, or who is likely to become a public charge

I think the hon. gentleman will agree to prevent the landing of persons of these classes. Very well. The Act goes on to say :
-and any person landed in Canada who, within two years thereafter, has become a charge upon the public funds, whether municipal, provincial or federal, or an inmate of, or a charge upon, any charitable institution, may be deported and returned to tlie^port or place whence he came or sailed for Canada.
Does the hon. gentleman admit that we have that power ?
Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman admits that we can exclude paupers, criminals, and those physically tainted or mentally unsound, whether they be British subjects or not. Well, if we exercise this power, why do we exercise it ? For our protection. ' The object of this Bill, as it has been stated, and as I tried to state it, is to create another cause of exclusion as recognized by the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) and the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) has given the reason for creating this new clause of exclusion. What is it 1 He says : The power vested in me is to prevent the entry of persons who are physically tainted, mentally unsound, criminals or paupers, and to send them back whence they come : but the power given me is nugatory unless the transportation company that brings such a person to'this country can take him to the place from which he came. The transpor-

tation company has taken, this immigrant on at Hong Kong. But, when he is returned, the authorities at Hong Kong refuse to receive him, and he is.Jeft between the two places like Mahomet's coffin hanging between heaven and earth. So, the Minister of the Interior seeks power to make effective the power that is given him. So far we understand each other. There is another question which the leader of the opposition has suggested, and that is whether we might not be going too far in this legislation, and whether we might not exclude another class of immigrants who ought to be admitted. That is a serious consideration. I do not know whether the Minister of the Interior has given his attention to it, but at all events it is a point worthy of consideration.

Touching the last point referred to by the Prime Minister, I will state the situation. As we all know, British Columbia is the province that has suffered most by the influx of Oriental immigrants. It is not desirable in the interest of British Columbia or in the interest of Canada that a class of people who cannot assimilate with any part of our own inhabitants should be permitted to come in without restriction. That I think ought to be admitted by every Canadian. Now what was the case in British Columbia before the order in council was passed ? We found Japanese agents on the one hand and Hindu agents on the other, practically starting a syndicate for the purpose of flooding British Columbia with Orientals- because our province was the objective point of all the immigrants who came from those countries. We find on the one hand the government of Japan saying that if Japanese leave their country and go to Honolulu or any other point, they are beyond the jurisdiction of the Japanese government, it has no control over them. On the other hand, we find the Hindu coming in, not from India but from another point between his native country and British Columbia. Now that had to be got over. I say it was in the interest, not only of British Columbia but of all of Canada, that some measure should be taken by which that immigration should be stopped. Now I want to say that I have hot been satisfied with what has been done, and I would have raised my voice time and again in this House if some means had not been taken to stop this wholesale influx. I do not care if the Hindu is a British subject. He may be a British subject, and have fought the battles of Great Britain on many occasions. He is a soldier and a good soldier, I admit all that; and I have as much respect for a British subject as any other man in this House, and I think I am as good a British subject, too. But I do not think this is imposing a hardship on those British
subjects coming straight from their native country to Canada, and if they do come direct and are desirable in every other respect, they would be allowed to land and become citizens of our country. But these men have been coming from Hong Kong, and why do they come ? They come simply at the instigation of these immigration agents who hold every man up who comes in, and levy upon him for bringing him into British Columbia. These men have inaugurated and are carrying out the profession of bringing immigrants into Canada, and reaping a benefit out of them in consequence. I say in all fairness, without wishing to reflect upon the Hindus, that they are not suitable citizens for British Columbia or for any other part of Canada ; they are not suited to the climate or to the work they are called upon to perform.
Won't thev find that out ?
We dont want thousands of them parading our streets trying to find that out. That is the position we take in British Columbia, and that is the position we will maintain.
And yet you will import Yankee hoodlums who are not even American citizens.

I am afraid my hon. friend must have suffered severe treatment from a Yankee hoodlum at some time. A point was made by the leader of the opposition and answered by the Prime Minister, that this Act might be made to apply to other classes of immigrants than Orientals. I do not think we need have any serious cause for fear that any considerable number of people will be excluded who come from other countries, under the operation of this Act if it becomes law. I think that is looking ahead for trouble which is not likely to happen. I have looked into the matter carefully, and I do not think that we in Canada need have any great fear that there will be any appreciable number of citizens of the United States, or Germany, or France, or any other country who wish to come in here, and who will be excluded under the provisions of this law. I know of no other way by which we can keep out these undesirable Orientals, and I have thought the matter over a good deal, unless you are going to discriminate against one or more nations. But if you put a provision of this kind in the law, all nations are then treated alike ; and all we ask of any nation, whether they be British subjects, or Frenchmen, or Germans, or any one else, is that they come direct from their own country to Canada. This Act will stop the machine work that has been going on in the case of the Japanese and Hindus, and those are the people we want to stop. As a British Columbian I say, and I main-

tain, that whether they are British subjects or not-and I give them every credit they deserve as British subjects-(British Columbia nor any other part of Canada is not a suitable country for Hindus, and it is not in the interest of British Columbia that they should come in in unrestricted numbers.

It seems to me that if we have a right to exclude British subjects for any reason whatever, either for mental or physical unsoundness, we have the absolute right to exclude them altogether. It is only a question whether it is judicious or not. ' For my part I sympathize with the evident desire of the Minister of the Interior to work out the problem that confronts him in this matter of immigration to British Columbia. I think it is very important that both sides of the House should address themselves to this matter, and endeavour to work out some way whereby this can be done without doing injustice to persons coming from other countries who may be desirable immigrants for Canada.

From the observations that I have been able to make, and from what I have heard living in a province adjoining British Columbia, I agree with the hon. member for Kootenay that the Hindus are not a desirable class of immigrants, and from what we have been able to learn up to the present time that class of immigration should not be encouraged. But I rose to my feet chiefly to refer to a remark of the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Macpherson) who has said that certain Japanese settlements have been satisfactory. I must apologise for introducing this matter in a discussion of this Bill, but I do it because the Minister of Labour is in his seat. I observe in a despatch from Edmonton, dated March 20, in which it is stated that fifty Japanese families will arrive in Calgary in a few days. I see another paragraph in the same paper, under the heading ' Jap farmers may not come this season, Strong feeling against Asiatics makes promoter hesitate.' Now as I understood the statement in this House of the Minister of Labour on a previous occasion, an arrangement had been come to with the Japanese government under which only students, travellers, and those who came over to Canada to visit their relatives, were to be admitted into this country. I simply mention this for the purpose of ascertaining whether it has come to the attention of the Minister of Labour. I desire to know if there have been 10,000 acres of land sold to Japanese in Southern Alberta, if these families are about to arrive and if there has been that satisfactory settlement to which he referred some - months ago how is it that these people are allowed to come in ?

I am aware that fifty Japanese families have been advertised to come to Canada shortly. All I know is that an understanding has been arrived at with the Japanese authorities, that the Japanese authorities have lived up to it until the present time, and I feel sure that the arrangement -which has been made will be carried out conscentiously by both sides. From the reports I have received from British Columbia, from the evidence that I receive every day from the representatives of that province in the House, the question seems to be settled, and there is now no influx of Japanese labourers into British Columbia. I have reason to believe that from this day on we will never hear of any such influx as that which took place last fall.

I think it will take a little more than the subtle remarks of the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. McCarthy) to galvanize into life that Japanese corpse. I do not think we will have the Japanese question as a factor in western Canada from this time on; that is, if Japan lives up to its agreement. I do not want to say anything that my hon. friend takes exception to, but I think that his little attempt to galvanize into life that Japanese corpse, because, as I said, I believe it is a corpse, will fail. I want to take exception to what the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Hughes) has said. He speaks of the Yankee hoodlums who come over here. I know that the Americans who come to this country make a most desirable class of citizens, and I know that the Hindus or any other class of Asiatics are not wanted in Canada. That line of cleavage is well marked and I think upon that line we can proceed; that is if we are going to keep Canada a white country.
Do you not want to keep it more than a white country ? Do you not want to keep it a decent country?
Yes, I do not think my hon. friend and I will quarrel about keeping it a decent country.
I would rather have a black gentleman thau a white anarchist.
I would too; I am not talking against black gentlemen.
There is a provision in the law against anarchists. _
It is not enforced.
It would be applied to Americans as well as other people.

I had reference to the galvanized Americans, the riff-raff who live for a short time in the United States and then come into Canada.
. Mr. MACPHERSON. A man who has been guilty of moral turpitude or of any 1 crime is kept out of Canada. We know

very 'well that it Is only the lowest possible caste that leave India and come to our shores. We do not get the Maharajas or the big people of India; they do not leave India on account of their caste.
, An hon. MEMBER. We do not get any nabobs.

We do not get any * nabobs. Some of them may have been soldiers. A man may be a first-class man and be a soldier and he may not be a first class man and be a soldier. Because a man has been a soldier it is no reason why we should admit him. There is no difficulty in getting a man to be a soldier in India because a Hindu would rather swell around in brass buttons than work. He does not like to work. Even if you are a British subject many times over and wear stripes and be a soldier that does not fit you to become a Canadian citizen of a type such as that to which wre believe Canadian citizens should conform. I think we can never expect to maintain a high standard of nationality unless we keep the strain white. The white man may not be just exactly the kind of man that you would like to invite into your parlour; he may not talk the language or understand it, but his boys and girls are going to school, they are given education along the required lines and they are singing ' God save the King ' and ' Rule Britannia ' within six months after they come here.
Are you not in danger if you draw the colour line ?

I would rather draw the colour line now than draw it fifty years later. If you read the history of the United States you will find that when they were flooding the southern states with Africans the same arguments were being used then, and it took years of fighting and bloodshed and millions of money to settle that question and it is not settled yet. It is far better for us to settle it now in the way in which we are attempting to settle It.

I do not propose that the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Macpherson) will get away with the insinuation that he has made that I am trying to resurrect the discussion on the Japanese question. That is not my intention. On the public Bills and orders there is a resolution of the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Smith) and if I had any desire to discuss the question further I would reserve my remarks until then. I simply pointed out to the hon. Minister of Labour that there appeared in a western paper a report that fifty Japanese proposed to land in Calgary within the next few days, and that 10,000 acres of land had been acquired by these people, together with the further statement that they might not come this season because there was a strong feeling against the promoters of this enterprise and they hesitated to bring them along. If there had been a report that these people 205
were coming to Vancouver instead of to Calgary the hon. member for Vancouver would have been the first man to get up in the House and try to find out if the report were true or not.

Since the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. McCarthy) has referred again to the number of Japanese who wish to settle near Calgary as agriculturists, I may say, in order to show that the Japanese authorities are living up to their agreement with Canada, that a few days ago the Canadian Pacific Railway Company applied to the Dominion government in order to ascertain if something like 300 Japanese would be allowed to enter the Dominion and take up land in the Northwest. The Canadian Pacific Railway authorities pointed out that the Japanese government would not object to issuing passports to the intending Japanese immigrants, but the Japanese government had stated that they could not issue passports unless the Dominion government would agree to it. That shows plainly that the Japanese authorities are living up to the agreement arrived at during the month of December last.

I want to call the government's attention to another matter in connection with the wording of this section. We have been dealing so far with the meaning of the last part of the clause which says:
Any immigrants who come to Canada otherwise than by continuous journey from the country of which they are natives or citizens and upon through tickets purchased in such country.
As the leader of the opposition has pointed out that appears to provide for the exclusion of a class that was not provided for until now. But the first part of the section provides for something distinct from that, and it says:
The Governor in Council may, by proclamation or order, whenever he considers it necessary or expedient, prohibit the landing in Canada of any specified class of immigrants.
Will the government explain what they expect that part of the clause to cover?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is subsection 1 of the Act as it exists at present.
I know.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We are merely repeating that subsection in the new Act and adding to it the provision which is under discussion. The provision referred to has never been applied so far and the fact that we are including it in this amendment does not indicate any immediate intention of applying it. There are very serious objections under ordinary circumstances to the application of an exclusion law against any class of people, and yet there may be occasions arising when it is desirable that such a



power should exist. From the time the Act was first passed we have never seen fit to exercise it, but we think it desirable that the power should still remain. It would only be exercised as a last resort.

We are giving the Governor in Council pretty extensive powers by that provision, although it may or may not be exercised. If you take it in the ordinary sense the provision would cover quite as large a class of persons as are provided for in the concluding words of the section. It is true the section was contained in the former Act, but these words were in addition:
Of which due notice shall he given to the transportation companies.
These words are now omitted. Then we had a subsection in the previous Act which we are now repealing and it is worth while remembering that. Subsection 2 provided that the Governor in Council might make such regulations as are necessary to prohibit the entry into Canada of any greater number of persons from any foreign country than the laws of such country permitted to emigrate to Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is not intended to repeal that.
Under the provision that the Governor in Council may prevent from landing any specified class of immigrants, could the Governor in Council issue a proclamation that Japanese shall not land in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That subsection was considered last year, and in consultation with the Justice Department we were advised that it was not a proper interpretation to put upon the word ' class,' to apply it to a nationality.

I am not prepared to argue that there is not some ground for that limitation or qualification, but at the same time I do not think it is any too clear. If the Governor in Council could make an order preventing the landing of Japanese it would be in direct conflict with the treaty with them. But it certainly would apply to the Governor in Council making a proclamation precluding carpenters or artisans or any specific class. The Minister of the Interior says yes. Then if that is so it would enable you to exclude Japanese artisans, and as I understand it we have not reserved the right in the treaty to exclude any class of Japanese from this country. If that be so we ought not to enact legislation which is inconsistent with the treaty with Japan. It is not that I want to circumscribe or hamper the efforts of the government in any way to preserve British Columbia as a white man's country, for I think that is one of the most desirable things we could aim at, but I am merely calling the attention of the gov-Mr. OLIVER.
eminent to legislation from that point of view.

I can reassure my hon. friend that by the agreement arrived at in the month of December with the Japanese authorities, all labour, skilled and unskilled is excluded. That is to say, they will be allowed to come into Canada only if the Canadian government accede to the request made by them to land in Canada, but they are excluded by the terms of the arrangement. I stated so when the question came up before.
I referred to Japanese labourers or artisans merely for illustration. But suppose for instance under this power to exclude a specified class it should be proposed to exclude Japanese students?
No.

If it means anything at all it means that the Governor in Council may exclude a limited class coming from any country, and in that way it could be made to include a class which would bring it in conflict with the treaty relations at present existing between Canada and Japan.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The answer to the point of my hon. friend, which was well taken in one sense, is this. Under this order in council the minister can exclude any class. For instance, suppose capitalists should be excluded, how would that work? It could not exclude Japanese capitalists, because they could invoke the treaty, which is superior to a statute of this House, as was decided by the British Columbia court in the case under the Natal Act. It was provided in that Act that any person coming to British Columbia should be subjected to an educational test. Under that provision some Japanese were arrested and convicted; but upon habeas corpus they were released, upon the ground alone that the legislation could not apply to Japanese, because they were protected by the treaty. Tne court did not go beyond that point, and I think this answers the point raised by my hon. friend.

Does not that place the government in another difficulty with regard to the words just now proposed to be added to the clause? The Prime Minister has stated accurately the effect of that decision, which amounted to this. Although the Natal Act might possibly apply to other nationalities, it could not apply to Japanese, not so much on account of the treaty, but on account of the Act of this parliament confirming the treaty, because provincial legislation with regard to immigration is always subject to legislation enacted by this parliament, and if it is repugnant to legislation enacted by this parliament, it has no effect. Does not the same objection apply to the words proposed

to be added? You propose to give tbe Governor in Council power * to prohibit the landing in Canada of any specified class of immigrants or of any Immigrants who being natives or citizens of any specified country have come to Canada otherwise than by a continuous' journey from that country on through tickets purchased there.' I would be inclined to think that any order in council issued under the authority of this statute would be inoperative so tar as Japanese subjects are concerned, for the very reason now given by the Prime Minister. Under the treaty subjects of the Empire of Japan have exactly the same right to enter, travel and reside in Canada as citizens of Canada have. Then you issue an order in council providing that persons coming under the conditions mentioned may be prohibited. That order in council may be very good as to all the nationalities of the world except the Japanese, but would it not be inoperative so far as they are concerned? Is that the way it is understood by the government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There is something in the point of my hon. friend. Though I think it might be met in another way, it is sufficient to observe at the present time that the Japanese authorities are aware that we attempt to exclude Japanese coming from Honolulu. They do not object to that. The Japanese authorities want their people to be treated in the same way as the people of any other civilized country, aud any law which we pass applying to all nations they do not object to.

The difficulty appears to have been overlooked by the Prime Minister and by the Minister of Labour, who spoke as if an arrangement with Japan would have the same effect as a treaty. The difficulty is that a Japanese subject coming to Vancouver and Victoria and being confronted by the order in council will simply take the same course as-was taken not long ago-apply to a solicitor and procure writ of habeas corpus, and the court will decide that the order in council has no application to him, and he therefore cannot be deported. It will not be a question between the government of Japan and the government of this country, but a question of the individual rights of the Japanese coming to this country, and invoking the statute of this parliament confirming the treaty.

If the legal interpretation given of the effect of the Japanese treaty is correct, then Japanese immigrants to Canada have a privilege which no British subject has. If it is true that no legislation of this House can supersede the terms of the treaty, then there is absolutely no control over the immigration of Japanese, and what is the good of an agreement with Japan? If that is the true legal position, 2051
the only alternative is to cancel the treaty. The spirit of the people of British Columbia is entirely against the immigration of Orientals. This legislation is no doubt extreme, but it is to remove an extreme evil; but if the legal opinion stated is correct that we cannot, by any regulations, orders in council or even legislation of this parliament, restrict or regulate the immigration of Orientals against the provisions of the treaty, then Canada has no control at all of immigration in the face of that treaty. I am not a lawyer, but that seems to me to be the situation, and the only proper conclusion is to cancel the treaty.

I would like to make myself plain to the hon. member for Nanaimo. Canada has, as I understand, very complete control of immigration by the very words of the British North America Act, which give us power to legislate in regard to it. AVe did legislate in regal'd to immigration from Japan when we passed an Act confirming the treaty made between Great Britain and Japan with respect to Canada. We could repeal that Act tomorrow. If we did repeal it, of course there would be an end of the treaty, because Japan would very properly take offence at that. AVe have agreed to confirm the treaty, and, having confirmed it, we could not, upon the principles of international usage, now pass an Act repealing the confirming Act of a year ago. AVe have now before us this statute, the terms of which might in their broadest signification be regarded as inconsistent with the Act of a year ago, especially with reference to Japan. They would not be held to be inconsistent, because in the Act of a year ago we were dealing with a specific subject, namely our relation to Japan, and this Act would not be held as repealing that Act because it deals with the whole subject of immigration. Therefore it seems to me that any order in council issued under this Act would be held, so far as Japan is concerned, to be subject to the Act of a year ago. That is all I intended to express.

I agree with the position taken by the First Alinister that we can pass this statute, but that where it conflicts with the treaty, the treaty will have force and this will not have force. But what I was calling the First Alinister's attention more particularly to was this. After passing an Act confirming a treaty, which prevents us from dealing with the Japanese question in this broad way, the question is whether it is wise for us to pass this Act without qualification. The First Minister says we are in effect tied hand and foot as regards Japan. I admit that. AVe cannot pass such broad legislation as this as regards Japan. I admit that. The hon. member for Nanaimo (Air. Ralph Smith) says that we cannot make laws upon this question. That being the case,

is it wise that we should pass this without qualification, without reference to the position in which we stand in relation to Japan ? As the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) says, a Japanese subject coming here, if arrested, goes into the court, and pleads his right. He does not plead that right on the basis of the understanding between the Minister of Labour (Mr. Le-mieux) and the Japanese government-we cannot set up that implied or verbal understanding-but what we are confronted with is the Japanese treaty, which over-rides the Act that we pass here, supersedes it, controls it and determines the rights of this Japanese subject. And he is released; that is the effect of it. Is it wise to enact legislation that, on the face of it, goes actually beyond what we have the power to enact ? I directed my remarks in the beginning to the first part of this clause, but they apply equally to the second part, though I did not wish to deal with that, as it has been so fully discussed. Nevertheless, I thought it well to call the attention of the government to the unfortunate position in which we are.

I agree with my hon. friend, so far as I am able to understand the legal point that this is in conflict with the Japanese treaty and cannot be enforced against the Japanese. Of course, I am not a lawyer and cannot say whether that is the legal effect of the position or not. But I understand it as the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Ralph Smith) stated it-that we have lost control so far as Japanese Immigration is concerned and that this Act would be futile in that respect. Now, I wish to call attention to another point. It would appear, upon the face of this clause that, when the government pass an order in council, a certain thing may be done. What I would like to know from the minister is this: Will this order in council become operative at once, or is notice to be given to the countries concerned? Suppose the order were passed to-morrow, but that a week ago, several shiploads of immigrants started for Canada from different countries which might be affected by this order. These people lawfully embarked, and the transportation companies lawfully undertook to transport them to Canada. If this order becomes operative at once, great injustice will be done to transportation companies and to immigrants who have spent their money for tickets only to find on their arrival here that an order in council has been passed under which they are to be sent back to the countries from which they came. Is due notice to be given, and, if so, what length of notice, to the steamship companies and Immigrants, before such a change In the law goes into operation?	*	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In the first place, I am bound to say that this proposed legislation is to go into effect, not by being passed by Mr. LENNOX.
the House, but by proclamation of the Governor in Council, and that it is the custom to give due notice before the passage of such an order in council.
Would the order in council be general or specific?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In any case, the order in council would affect the transportation companies and immigrants, and it is only right and reasonable that there should be notice. And notice has been given in the past and will be in the future. My hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) mentioned that in the Act as it stands there is a provision that due notice shall be given, and that these words are not contained in the measure as it stands now before the House. The reason for leaving out these words is that when they are placed in the statute, there is the question as to what 'due notice ' is, and this might lead to very serious complications. Therefore, we believe it is better that the government should be trusted to give due notice rather than that words should be put in the statute that would be difficult of interpretation, and might render of none effect the intent of parliament and the action of the government.
In regard to the point which has been under discussion, raised by my hon. friend from South Simcoe-concerning which, perhaps, I have not the same license as members of the legal profession-I must say that the matter does not strike me as they have presented it to the House. It seems to me elementary that the parliament of Canada is supreme within Canada; that whatever parliament has done parliament can undo, that, if, last year, we passed an Act which gave certain privileges to certain people, we can, this year, pass as Act which does not give these privileges to these people, and that Act is valid so far as the courts of Canada are concerned and so far as it affects the people within the boundaries of Canada.
Is this intended as being pro tanto a repeal of the Act of last year confirming the treaty with Japan?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No. I am maintaining, as concerning the Bill before the House, that it does not repeal the Act of last session.
That is what I contended also.
That is what we all contend.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: But our friends pretend that the intent is to repeal-
No, I did not.
On the contrary, I agreed with the First Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) when he said the treaty would be more powerful than this, that the treaty would prevail against this Act.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have not been able to get my point understood yet. As I understand our friends opposite, they maintain that the Act of last session regarding the Japanese treaty stood effective against this Act which we propose to pass this session.
That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Well, I say that the matter does not appeal to me in that way. As I said before, the parliament of Canada is supreme within the limits of Canada. The parliament of Canada passed an Act last session with regard to the Japanese treaty. So far as the people of Canada are concerned within the limits of Canada, an Act passed by the parliament of Canada at this session is effective and binding upon the courts of Canada, whether it is or is not contrary to the legislation passed.
That is what I asked-was this statute intended to repeal the Act of last session in that respect, and the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) said, ' no.'

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I said, in my estimation. A)1 these matters must be matters of opinion. In my estimation this does not purport to repeal ; but if it did, then I maintain that if this parliament passed it, it would repeal.
If appropriate words were used, it certainly would repeal, but appropriate words are not used.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have rather missed the point of our friends argument or they have missed mine. My understanding is that if this legislation is passed, it will be effective. It will have effect in law and be binding upon the courts as it is expressed, without regard to the terms of the treaty passed last session.

My hon. friend has said exactly the contrary. He has declared that this Act is not intended to repeal or affect in any way the Act of last year and therefore the order in council proposed to be passed must be subject to the treaty of last year. That is an absolute logical conclusion. You cannot get away from it. This Bill is not intended to repeal the Act of last year.
Because it is not necessary. The Japanese government have come to an understanding which makes it absolutely unnecessary.

I am surprised that my hon. friend the Minister of Labour would repeat that twice. Does he not know that any Japanese coming to British Columbia can avail himself of that treaty, absolutely in disregard of any informal arrangement made between this government and the government of .Japan? I did not think I would have to explain that even to any member who does not belong to the legal profession. There is a treaty between the
two nations, which treaty is confirmed by the parliament of Canada. That treaty derives its force in this country altogether from the legislation of this parliament last year, and to suggest that the Minister of Labour and the Japanese Minister of Foreign Affairs can repeal, by an understanding between them, the legislation confirming this treaty is so utterly absurd, that I would not think any one would for one moment entertain such a suggestion.

There is a treaty binding upon this country and Japan, but we know that no Japanese subject can leave a port of Japan without the express authority of the Japanese government, and he cannot come to this country against that authority.

My hon. friend has not been paying attention or he would know that that is not the point. I am speaking of Japanese coming from Hawaii. These are the men to whom the statute would apply and not those who come from Japan.
I might point out what is absolutely obvious. These men coming from Hawaii to British Columbia could invoke that treaty with an absolute disregard of any arrangement made by the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Japan. The treaty between the Empire of Japan and this country has been confirmed by the parliament of Canada. It is the legislation affirming that treaty which binds Canada, and not any arrangement such as is spoken of by the Minister of Labour. How ridiculous would it not be for any counsel in a British Columbia court to argue, in opposition to a motion for the release of these men that the treaty which gives every Japanese subject the absolute right to enter, travel and reside in Canada has been repealed by an arrangement between the Minister of Labour of Canada and the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Japan, and therefore these men must be deported. Even a one year's law student, who valued his reputation, would not make such an argument as that.
Who suggested that ?

I understood the Minister of Labour to suggest it. I do not know what he did suggest, if he did not intend that. When the legislation was invoked, my hon. friend put forward the operative force of an arrangement made himself with the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Japan.

Not its operative force before our courts. What I say is that the necessity for such deportation will not arise, and consequently there will be no case before our courts and no necessity for invoking this treaty as against the arrangement with Japan. My hon. friend contends

that the treaty may be availed of by any Japanese subject before our courts. But what I reply is that such a possibility is a very remote one indeed. True there is the treaty, but there is also the understanding-not a verbal understanding, as suggested by my hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) but a written one-with the Japanese government, under which no immigration can take place except in compliance with that arrangement. No Japanese will be allowed to leave Japan without a passport. My hon. friend suggests that a Japanese might come from the Sandwich Islands and not direct from Japan and might invoke the treaty before our courts. But he is still a Japanese subject, and if he came in contravention of the arrangement between Japan and Canada, he would be acting against the laws of his own country, and the Canadian government would be in a position to deport him.

That suggestion would be very valuable indeed if the laws of Japan were in force in Canada, but unfortunately they are not. It is the laws of this parliament which are-in force in Canada. Therefore a Japanese subject coming from Hawaii can depend on the terms of the treaty because that treaty has been affirmed by an Act of this parliament. It would be absolutely idle to suggest that any arrangement, whether verbal or written, whether under seal or not, made between our Minister of Labour and the Foreign Minister of Japan, could have the slightest effect on the legal status of that man entering this country from Hawaii. It is absolute nonsense to suppose that such would be the case. Therefore the question comes back to the point from which we started a moment ago. The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) admits, and properly admits, that this proposed legislation cannot and does not purport to repeal our statute of last year confirming the treaty between Canada and Japan.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What I meant to say. was that it does not purport to repeal that treaty but it could if we wanted It to.

Certainly this parliament can repeal the Act of last year but we are not doing it, and it is idle to discuss the effect of something we are not doing. Let us discuss what we are doing. We are simply leaving the Japanese treaty where it was when we passed that Act confirming it. Therefore any order in council put forth under the terms of this proposed legislation could not in the slightest degree affect the provisions of the Japanese treaty confirmed by an Act of this parliament.
It has been done in British Columbia by the courts there. Two Japanese were deported to the United States under that order in council.

I am referring to the decision of the courts of British Columbia alluded to by the right hon. gentleman. We have arrived at the point where we are all agreed that this proposed legislation does not touch the Act of last year. There is but one point to be considered, a point mentioned by the right hon. gentleman, whether an order in council providing that persons not coming in by a continuous journey or on a through ticket, should be deported, would apply to citizens of Japan. The decision of the British Columbia courts indicates that such an order in council would be subject to the Act of last year, and that the operation of the Act of last year would exempt citizens of Japan from the operation of such an order.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is now six o'clock, and I have only this to say, that according to international law I think no treaty prevents one of the contracting parties from exercising the power vested in it to pass municipal regulations necessary for its own protection. For instance, though we have a treaty here, I am quite sure we can exclude a Japanese who is mentally or physically diseased, and if we can do that, we have power to do by legislation all that is necessary to carry out this provision of municipal law, and that is what we intend to do.

A moment ago, the right hon. gentleman nodded his assent to the proposition of the hon. member for King's that because we have a qualified power to restrict these persons coming from the British isles, therefore we have power of absolute restriction-if he should attempt to apply this argument in the case of Japan, he would be confronted by the treaty.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We have power to enforce our own municipal regulations for our own protection. At all events, that is the position we have taken on this question, and we believe it to be legal. I move the previous question.
I would have liked an opportunity to discuss this matter further.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I would like very much to send this Bill to the Senate so that they may act upon it before they adjourn, the Senate adjourns to-morrow. This is very important legislation for British Columbia.
I want to say a few words more.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext:
The Prime Minister has not shown any necessity for the legislation.
Mr. MACPH 10RSOX. I think there is need of immediate legislation, in the best interest of British Columbia. I trust the House will see fit to meet the Prime Minister's wishes so that this Bill may go to the Senate and become operative at once. There is a crying necessity for it. Is the hon. gentleman prepared to accept the responsibility of delaying legislation which will prevent these yellow people from coming into our province ? What did the leader of the opposition say in British Columbia ? He stood for a white man's country.

If the hon. gentleman is going to make a stump speech here, he is taking the best means of holding up this Bill. As a matter of fact I object to this Bill going through at the present time. The hon. gentleman was not taking a manly part in British Columbia on this question. We were standing here on this question. We were standing here in defence of a better citizenship.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman cannot make a speech.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If the House is not willing to consent to pass this measure now. we have nothing to do but to adjourn.

I want to put myself on record that I am in favour of a white man's country, and also in favour of a decent country.
Progress reported.
What legislation will be taken up to-morrow ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Bill of the Minister of Inland Revenue and the two Bills of the Minister of Railways.
Will this matter be taken up again to-morrow ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes.
House adjourned at six o'clock.

Thursday, April 9, 1908.
